part_title: GenAI Analytics Architecture and Amazon Athena

scenes.title: Analytics for GenAI applications
scenes.narration: This opening slide connects the data generated by a GenAI application to decisions that actually improve it. Follow the three stages: raw application data lands in Amazon S3; Athena or EMR prepares and analyses that data; QuickSight turns the results into interactive dashboards. The source examples include user interactions, application logs, traces, model evaluation results and reference metadata. Don't assume raw prompts and full responses should be logged indiscriminately: sensitive content needs minimisation and protection before entering a data lake. On the right, the dashboard groups operating metrics such as request volume and P-fifty and P-ninety-five latency with model-quality indicators: relevance, groundedness, toxicity and hallucination rates. These measure different things. A technically fast response could still be unsupported or unsafe. Now look at the three roles along the bottom. Data engineers build curated datasets, analysts explore use patterns, and ML or GenAI engineers use evaluation findings to improve retrieval, prompts and models. This is an analytics feedback loop: capture permitted evidence, process it into trustworthy measurements, expose trends and make validated changes.

scenes.title: Amazon Athena Query Flow
scenes.narration: Read this Athena diagram as a four-stage query. First, a user submits standard SQL, here asking for order counts grouped by product category since the beginning of 2024. Athena consults the AWS Glue Data Catalog for table definitions, column types, partitions and S3 locations. With that metadata, Athena reads relevant data files from S3, applies filtering and aggregation, and writes the result set back to a configured S3 query-results location. The example table lists category counts, such as Electronics ahead of Home and Books. Athena is serverless from the query user's perspective: you don't administer a long-running SQL cluster. That does not mean query design and storage layout are irrelevant. Partition pruning and columnar formats such as Parquet can greatly reduce the amount of data scanned, improving cost and speed. The query-running role also needs appropriate Glue, Athena, S3 and possibly KMS permissions. One important boundary: Athena reads and queries datasets; it is not a transactional application database. Use it when you want SQL analytics over an S3 data lake.

scenes.title: Athena use cases for GenAI
scenes.narration: This slide puts Athena into a GenAI question-answering workflow. Start with a business question about top product categories in a quarter. A model can translate the permitted question into SQL, then a service executes that SQL through Athena against sales data in S3. Other S3 objects, such as product documentation or FAQs, can supply contextual evidence through a separate retrieval path. The application combines validated query results and relevant text passages before generating an answer with source references. It is important not to conflate the two operations: Athena performs the SQL analysis; retrieving document chunks requires an appropriate retrieval or indexing mechanism. Now examine the lower monitoring panels. The application records request status, timestamps, token usage, latency, estimated cost and evaluation scores such as relevance, groundedness and safety. Those metrics let teams investigate whether answers are useful as well as whether the pipeline runs successfully. Never execute unconstrained model-generated SQL as a privileged user: validate queries, restrict accessible catalogs and tables, and enforce tenant permissions before execution. The takeaway is governed analytics plus grounded response generation, followed by measurable quality checks.
